chapter.title: Placing your first order

cards.body: You walk up to a stall in the bazaar and say what you want. You can say *buy now, whatever the going rate is*, or *buy, but only if it's ₹500 or less, and if not, I'll wait*. That one sentence is your **order**, and your broker is the runner who carries it to the counter.
cards.simpler: Think of a market stall. You walk up and say what you want. You can say buy now at today's price. Or you can say buy only if it costs ₹500 or less, and if not, I'll wait. That one sentence is your **order**. Your broker is the runner who carries your order to the counter for you.

cards.prompt: A chai stall's price flips between ₹10 and ₹12 every few seconds. You tell your friend: 'get me one, but only if it's ₹10.' It stays at ₹12. What happens?

options.text: Your friend buys at ₹12 anyway. You did say 'get me one'.
Your friend waits. No chai until ₹10 shows up.
Your friend pays ₹10 and argues the stall into it.

whyNot.a: That's a market order, not a limit: 'get me one' with no price means pay whatever is showing.
whyNot.c: A limit order waits for your price. It doesn't force the seller down to it.

cards.reteach: A limit is a line you draw: this much and no more. If nobody will sell at that line, nothing happens and your money stays with you. Only a market order says 'any price, just do it now'.

cards.title: Two ways to say buy
cards.body:
A *market order* means buy now at whatever the next seller is asking. It fills in a second. The catch: the price you get can be a few rupees off the one you saw, because the screen moves while your order travels.

A *limit order* means buy only at your price or better. You type ₹500, so you pay ₹500 or less, never more. If no seller comes down to ₹500, the order sits open until 3:30 pm and then cancels.

**Limit orders trade speed for certainty.** For your first share, certainty is the better deal.
cards.simpler: A market order means buy now at whatever the next seller asks. It fills fast. The price can be a few rupees off what you saw, because prices move while your order travels. A limit order means buy only at your price or lower. Type ₹500 and you pay ₹500 or less, never more. If nobody sells at ₹500, the order waits until 3:30 pm, then cancels. **Limit orders trade speed for certainty.** For a first share, certainty wins.

cards.title: Meera's ₹2 and 11 minutes
cards.body: Meera wants 1 share of an IT company on the Nifty 50. The screen says ₹1,520. She types a limit order for 1 share at ₹1,518 and picks *delivery*, which means she intends to keep the share, not sell it by evening. **Nothing happens for 11 minutes.** Then the price dips, the order fills at ₹1,518, and she has saved ₹2, learned what *pending* means, and spent 11 minutes staring at her phone. Worth it, she says.
cards.simpler: Meera wants 1 share of an IT company on the Nifty 50. The screen shows ₹1,520. She types a limit order for 1 share at ₹1,518. She picks delivery, which means she plans to keep the share, not sell it the same day. **Nothing happens for 11 minutes.** Then the price dips and her order fills at ₹1,518. She saved ₹2, learned what pending means, and spent 11 minutes staring at her phone. Worth it, she says.

cards.prompt: Ravi wants 1 share of a Nifty 50 cement company. The screen shows ₹2,350. He'd happily pay ₹2,350 but not a rupee more, and he doesn't mind waiting. Which order?

options.text: Limit order, 1 share, price ₹2,300, to save ₹50.

whyNot.a: That's the 'any price, right now' option: it might fill at ₹2,352, which is the rupee more he refused.
whyNot.c: That's a limit below the market: it only fills if the price drops ₹50, which may never happen today. He said ₹2,350 was fine.

cards.reteach: The limit price is the most you'll pay. Set it at the price you're happy with. Above it, you overpay. Far below it, you may wait forever.

cards.title: When it lands, and what it costs
cards.body:
Your order fills, but the share isn't in your demat locker yet. India settles trades on *T+1*: T is the trade day, so the share arrives the next working day. Buy on Friday, see it on Monday. The money leaves your trading account at once.

Every trade carries small charges: *brokerage* (the broker's fee, ₹0 for delivery at many discount brokers), *STT* (securities transaction tax, 0.1% of the buy value), plus tiny stamp duty, exchange fees and GST. **On 1 share of ₹1,500, the total is usually a few rupees.** The exact breakup arrives that night in an email called a *contract note*.
cards.simpler: Your order fills, but the share reaches your demat account only the next working day. That rule is called T+1. Buy on Friday, see it Monday. The money leaves at once. Brokerage is the broker's fee, often ₹0 for delivery. STT is a 0.1% tax on the buy value. Tiny stamp duty, exchange fees and GST add on. **On 1 share of ₹1,500, the total is usually a few rupees.** A contract note email that night lists it all.

cards.body: Arjun saw a share at ₹870 and typed a limit order for ₹800, thinking the discount was free. He checked every hour. At 3:30 pm the order quietly cancelled, and he decided the app was broken. Spot it: an order marked *open* or *pending* **is not a bug**. It's the bazaar telling you nobody will sell at your line yet.
cards.simpler: Arjun saw a share at ₹870 and typed a limit order for ₹800. He thought the discount came free. He checked every hour. At 3:30 pm the order quietly cancelled, and he decided the app was broken. Here is the lesson. An order marked open or pending **is not a bug**. It is the market telling you nobody wants to sell at your price yet.

cards.prompt: Which line, said at the counter, is a market order?

options.text: 'One share, whatever it's going for right now.'
'One share, but only once it lands in my demat tomorrow.'

whyNot.a: That's the limit order: a price line, and patience.
whyNot.c: That's T+1 settlement, not an order type: the share landing next day happens after any order fills.

cards.reteach: Market order: no price, instant fill, small surprise possible. Limit order: your price, possible wait, no surprise. Settlement is separate: whichever you pick, the share reaches your locker the next working day.

cards.title: In one breath
cards.body: A market order buys now at whatever price is showing; a limit order buys only at your price or better, and **waits if it has to**. The share lands in your demat the next working day, and the charges on 1 share come to a few rupees.
cards.simpler: A market order buys now at whatever price is showing. A limit order buys only at your price or better, and **waits if it has to**. The share lands in your demat account the next working day. The charges on 1 share come to a few rupees.

cards.body: Open your broker app, pick any Nifty 50 share, tap Buy, and switch between Market and Limit without placing anything. **Notice which one asks for a price.** Then close it.
cards.simpler: Open your broker app. Pick any share from the Nifty 50 list. Tap Buy. Now switch between Market and Limit, but do not place anything. **Notice which one asks you for a price.** That is the whole exercise. Then close the app.

chapter.outcomeLine: You can now buy 1 share with a limit order, say when it lands in your demat, and list the charges you paid.
